A US Navy codebreaking “bombe,” built to break the German navy’s Enigma. Photo: National Security Agency, public domain.

DECLASSIFIED

Secrets of WWII

Codebreakers, spies and tricks; The hidden front of World War II

A mini lesson before you play Codebreakers: The Hidden War

Before we play the game, a short mini lesson. These are real stories from World War II: the codebreakers, the spies and the tricks that helped decide the war. Some of them are in the game, and some are not. All of them really happened.

Warm-up

Myth or fact?

Germany’s Enigma machine was unbreakable.

MYTH

Polish mathematicians broke it in 1932, and Britain read it for much of the war.

Codebreakers were found with a newspaper crossword.

FACT

In 1942, people who solved a Daily Telegraph crossword in under 12 minutes were invited to secret tests.

Most of Bletchley Park’s staff were men.

MYTH

About three-quarters of them were women.

A coded WWII pigeon message has never been read.

FACT

It was found in an English chimney in 2012, and nobody has decoded it.

Warm-up. Read each statement and have students vote: myth or fact? Then click to reveal each answer. One: Enigma was unbreakable. Myth: Polish mathematicians broke it in 1932, and Britain read it for much of the war. Two: codebreakers were found with a crossword. Fact: in 1942, people who solved a newspaper crossword in under 12 minutes were invited to secret tests. Three: most of Bletchley Park's staff were men. Myth: about three-quarters were women. Four: a coded pigeon message from the war has never been read. Fact: it was found in a chimney in 2012. We will come back to all of these.

An Enigma machine at the NSA’s National Cryptologic Museum. Photo: Dave Ley, public domain.

Did you know? · The codebreakers

A machine with too many settings

159,000,000,000,000,000,000

That’s about how many ways an army Enigma could be set up, and the settings changed every day.

  • 1932: Polish mathematician Marian Rejewski breaks it using math.
  • 1939: Poland shares its methods with Britain and France.
  • 1940 onward: Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman’s “bombe” machines test settings at speed.
This is a real Enigma machine, now in the US National Cryptologic Museum. You typed a letter on the keyboard, and a different letter lit up on the lampboard. It could be set up in about 159 million million million different ways, and the settings changed every day at midnight. The Germans were sure nobody could read it. But in 1932 a young Polish mathematician, Marian Rejewski, broke it using mathematics. In July 1939, weeks before the war, Poland shared its methods and replica machines with Britain and France. At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman designed machines called bombes that could test settings far faster than people could.

Did you know? · The codebreakers

Hired by crossword

12 min

In January 1942, readers complained that the Daily Telegraph crossword was too easy. A challenge followed: solve one under timed conditions in 12 minutes.

What happened next

People who finished in time were later contacted and invited to more tests. Some went on to secret codebreaking work for the war.

Why a crossword?

Codebreaking needed the same skills: patterns, patience, guessing a word from a few letters, and staying calm under time pressure.

Discuss: would you have made it? What other everyday skills could help a codebreaker?

Here's a true story. In January 1942, readers wrote to the Daily Telegraph newspaper to complain that its crossword was too easy. So a challenge was set up: solve a crossword under timed conditions in 12 minutes. Some of the people who finished in time were later quietly contacted and invited to more tests, and some went on to do secret codebreaking work. Crosswords use the same skills as codebreaking: spotting patterns, guessing a word from a few letters, and staying calm under pressure. Ask: would you have made it?

Did you know? · The codebreakers

A secret army of women

75%

By 1945, nearly 10,000 people worked at Bletchley Park and its outstations. About three-quarters of them were women.

10,000+

In the United States, more than 10,000 women worked as codebreakers for the Army and Navy.

Sworn to secrecy

They signed secrecy oaths, and many never told their own families what they had done until decades later.

Most people picture codebreakers as men in suits, but most of the codebreaking workforce was women. By 1945 nearly 10,000 people worked at Bletchley Park and its outstations, and about three-quarters of them were women. They ran the bombe machines, sorted and translated messages, and broke codes themselves. In the United States, more than 10,000 women worked as Army and Navy codebreakers. They signed oaths of secrecy, and many kept the secret for decades, even from their own families.

Did you know? · The codebreakers

The computer nobody knew about

In 1944, engineer Tommy Flowers and his team built Colossus. It is often called the world’s first programmable electronic computer.

  • Its job: break “Tunny,” the cipher of Hitler’s high command.
  • By 1945: ten machines, working day and night.
  • After the war: most were broken up, and the secret was kept until the 1970s.

Dorothy Du Boisson and Elsie Booker operating Colossus. Photo: UK National Archives, public domain.

Here's a surprise: one of the first computers was built to break codes, and almost nobody knew. In this photo, two members of the Women's Royal Naval Service, Dorothy Du Boisson and Elsie Booker, are operating Colossus. Engineer Tommy Flowers and his team built it in 1944 to help read Tunny, the cipher used by Hitler's high command, which was even harder than Enigma. By the end of the war there were ten Colossus machines. Afterwards most were broken up and the secret was kept until the 1970s, so for years other computers got the credit for being first.

Spotlight · Spies and deceivers

Garbo: the spy who invented spies

Juan Pujol García, code-named GARBO by the British and ARABEL by the Germans, in disguise. Photo: MI5 / UK National Archives, public domain.

  • He offered to spy for Britain and was turned down, so he got the Germans to hire him instead.
  • Working from Lisbon, he made up reports about Britain using a guidebook, maps, a railway timetable and newsreels.
  • In 1942 he reached London, and MI5 ran him and his 27 imaginary agents. Germany paid them all.
  • He received a German Iron Cross and a British MBE, probably the only person given both.
  • In 1949 he faked his own death and was not found again until 1984.

His biggest lie came in 1944. MI5 players will find out in the game.

Meet Garbo, one of the strangest spies in history. This photo from MI5's files shows him in disguise. Juan Pujol García was a Spaniard who hated the Nazis. He offered to spy for Britain and was turned down, so he talked the Germans into hiring him instead. From Lisbon, he invented reports about Britain using a guidebook, maps, a railway timetable and newsreels, and the Germans believed him. In 1942 he reached London, where MI5 ran him with his case officer Tomás Harris and a network of 27 imaginary agents, all paid by Germany. The British code-named him Garbo; the Germans called him Arabel. He was awarded both a German Iron Cross and a British MBE. After the war he faked his death and disappeared until a writer tracked him down in 1984. Don't give away what he did in 1944: that is part of the MI5 role in the game.

Spotlight · Spies and deceivers

The man who never was

  • To hide the real target, Sicily, British officers Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley planned to fool Germany with a dead body carrying fake invasion plans.
  • The body was a homeless Welshman, Glyndwr Michael, given a whole fake life.
  • His pockets held theater ticket stubs, love letters from “Pam” with her photo (really an MI5 clerk), and a bank letter about his overdraft.
  • On 30 April 1943 a British submarine released him off Spain, and a Spanish fisherman found him.
  • When Germany fell for it, Churchill was told: “Mincemeat swallowed rod, line and sinker.”

FORGED

The fake ID card of “Major William Martin.” The photo isn’t the dead man: it’s an MI5 officer, Ronnie Reed, who looked like him. Source: Ewen Montagu, 1953, public domain.

This is one of the most famous tricks of the war, and it's in the game. In 1943 the Allies were about to invade Sicily, and Germany knew Sicily was the obvious target. British intelligence officers Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley came up with a plan: a dead body dressed as a British officer, carrying fake letters about invading Greece and Sardinia instead. The body was a homeless Welshman named Glyndwr Michael. They gave "Major William Martin" a whole life: theater ticket stubs, love letters from a fiancée called Pam, with a photo that was really of an MI5 clerk, even a letter from his bank about money he owed. Look at the ID card: the photo on it isn't the dead man at all, but an MI5 officer, Ronnie Reed, who looked a bit like him. A British submarine released the body off the coast of Spain on 30 April 1943, and a Spanish fisherman found it. German intelligence believed the papers and sent reinforcements to Greece and Sardinia. Churchill was told: "Mincemeat swallowed rod, line and sinker."

Spotlight · Spies and deceivers

Virginia Hall: the limping lady

  • An American from Baltimore, she lost part of her left leg in a 1933 hunting accident and walked on an artificial leg she nicknamed “Cuthbert.”
  • From 1941, working for Britain’s SOE, she organized resistance networks in occupied France, finding safe houses and helping agents escape.
  • The Gestapo hunted her. In late 1942 she escaped by crossing the Pyrenees mountains on foot in winter.
  • She came back in 1944 for the American OSS to train resistance fighters around the time of D-Day.
  • She was the only civilian woman awarded the US Distinguished Service Cross in World War II.

Virginia Hall receiving the Distinguished Service Cross, September 1945. Photo: CIA, public domain.

Virginia Hall was an American from Baltimore. After losing part of her left leg in a hunting accident, she walked on an artificial leg she called Cuthbert. Even so, she became one of the most important Allied agents in occupied France. Working first for Britain's Special Operations Executive, she built resistance networks, found safe houses and helped agents escape. The Gestapo hunted her as "the limping lady." In late 1942 she escaped over the Pyrenees mountains to Spain on foot, in winter. She went back to France in 1944 for the American OSS to train resistance fighters around D-Day. This photo shows her receiving the Distinguished Service Cross in 1945: she was the only civilian woman to receive it in World War II. In the game, she is one of the real people behind the Resistance Courier role.

Spotlight · The Ultimate Deception

The Ghost Army

A US Army unit of about 1,100 soldiers whose job was to look like a much bigger army.

  • Fake tanks: inflatable rubber tanks and trucks that looked real from the air.
  • Fake sounds: huge speakers played recordings of tanks and troops at night.
  • Real artists: including future fashion designer Bill Blass and painter Ellsworth Kelly.

From June 1944 to March 1945 they staged more than 20 deceptions across Europe. In 2024 the unit received the Congressional Gold Medal.

An inflatable dummy Sherman tank, the kind of decoy the Ghost Army used. Photo: Imperial War Museums, public domain.

The Ghost Army was a real US Army unit of about 1,100 soldiers, and its job was to fool the Germans into seeing armies that weren't there. The photo shows an inflatable dummy Sherman tank, the kind of decoy they used: from the air it looked real. They also played recordings of tanks and soldiers through huge speakers at night, and sent fake radio messages. Many of them were artists and designers, including Bill Blass, who later became a famous fashion designer, and the painter Ellsworth Kelly. Between June 1944 and March 1945 they carried out more than 20 deception missions across France, Belgium, Luxembourg and Germany. Their work stayed secret for decades, and in 2024 the unit was awarded the Congressional Gold Medal. In the game, the fake army before D-Day uses the same kind of trick.

A WAAF wireless operator taking down a Morse code message, the same job the listeners did. Photo: RAF / Imperial War Museums, public domain.

More roles in the secret war

The listeners

  • Before anyone could break a code, someone had to catch the message. Britain’s “Y Service” listeners tuned in to enemy radio day and night.
  • They wrote down every Morse code letter by hand, even though the messages looked like nonsense to them.
  • Many were young women in the women’s services of the navy, army and air force.
  • The messages went to Bletchley Park by motorcycle courier and teleprinter.
  • One missed letter could make a message impossible to break, so accuracy mattered more than speed.

In the game, every intercept you decrypt was first caught by someone like this.

Codebreakers could only break what someone had first heard. The Y Service was Britain's network of radio listening stations. Operators, many of them young women in the women's branches of the navy, army and air force, sat with headphones for hours, writing down enemy Morse code letter by letter. The photo shows a WAAF wireless operator doing exactly that kind of work. The messages meant nothing to them, because they were in code, but one missed letter could make a message much harder to break. The intercepts were rushed to Bletchley Park by motorcycle dispatch riders and later by teleprinter. Most of these listeners never knew what happened to the messages they took down.

More roles in the secret war

The coastwatchers

Coastwatchers outside their radio hut on Guadalcanal. Photo: Australian War Memorial, public domain.

  • Australian and British officers, helped by local islanders, hid in the hills and jungles of islands like the Solomons, behind enemy lines.
  • When Japanese planes or ships passed, they radioed a warning, giving Allied fighters time to get ready.
  • Their warnings helped the Allies hold on at Guadalcanal in 1942.
  • In 1943, islanders Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana found the stranded crew of PT-109, including future president John F. Kennedy, and coastwatchers arranged their rescue.

In the game, the cover story after Yamamoto’s plane is shot down points to coastwatchers.

The coastwatchers were Allied lookouts hidden on Pacific islands that Japan had captured. The photo shows a group of them outside their radio hut on Guadalcanal. Most were Australian or British officers who knew the islands well, and they depended completely on local islanders for food, guides and protection. From hiding places in the hills, they radioed warnings whenever Japanese planes or ships went past, which gave Allied pilots time to get into the air. Their warnings were a big help during the long battle for Guadalcanal in 1942. In 1943, two islanders, Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana, found the stranded crew of the torpedo boat PT-109, including a young officer named John F. Kennedy, and coastwatchers arranged the rescue. In the game, the Americans let people believe coastwatchers had spotted Yamamoto, to hide that the code had been broken.

More roles in the secret war

The secret radio operator

  • In June 1943, Noor Inayat Khan, code name Madeleine, became the first woman radio operator sent into occupied France by Britain’s SOE.
  • Radio operators sent messages to London in Morse code from hidden sets. German detector vans hunted their signals, so they had to keep moving.
  • When her network was broken up, she refused to come home and became one of the last links between Paris and London.
  • She was betrayed and arrested that October, and killed at Dachau in 1944. She never gave away her secrets, and was awarded the George Cross.

The Resistance Courier role in the game faces the same danger: every message is a risk.

Noor Inayat Khan, 1943. Photo: Imperial War Museums, public domain.

Agents in occupied Europe needed a way to talk to London, and that job belonged to secret radio operators. They tapped out Morse code on radio sets hidden in suitcases, while German detector vans drove the streets trying to find their signals, so they had to keep moving and stay on the air as briefly as possible. Noor Inayat Khan, shown here in 1943, code name Madeleine, became the first woman radio operator sent into occupied France by Britain's Special Operations Executive, in June 1943. When her network was broken up, she refused to leave, and for a time she was one of the last links between Paris and London. She was betrayed and arrested in October 1943, and killed at Dachau concentration camp in 1944. She never revealed her secrets. She was awarded the George Cross, Britain's highest civilian award for bravery, after the war. This is a serious story; it shows how dangerous this work was.

More roles in the secret war

The photo detectives

An RAF spy-plane photo of Peenemünde, 23 June 1943. A: a V-2 rocket on its trailer. B: a mobile test stand. C: the assembly hall. Photo: RAF, public domain.

  • Unarmed spy planes flew over enemy territory and took millions of photographs. Interpreters at RAF Medmenham, west of London, studied them.
  • With a stereoscope, two photos side by side popped into 3D, so they could measure buildings and weapons.
  • In 1943, interpreter Constance Babington Smith spotted a tiny flying bomb on a launch ramp at Peenemünde, Germany’s secret weapons base.
  • Photos also helped plan D-Day, checking beaches, defenses and bridges.

In the game, Resistance Couriers smuggle out proof about the same rocket program.

Not all intelligence came from radio messages. RAF reconnaissance planes, stripped of guns so they could fly higher and faster, photographed enemy territory, and the photos went to the Central Interpretation Unit at RAF Medmenham, a country house west of London. This is one of those real photos: Peenemünde on 23 June 1943. Point out label A: that small shape is a V-2 rocket lying on its trailer. Interpreters, many of them women, studied pictures like this under magnifiers. Using a stereoscope, two overlapping photos could be seen in 3D, so they could measure the size of buildings and weapons. Later in 1943, interpreter Constance Babington Smith spotted a tiny aircraft-shaped object on a launch ramp at Peenemünde: one of Germany's secret flying bombs. Photo interpreters also helped plan D-Day. In the game, the Resistance Courier role tracks the same secret rocket program from the ground.

More roles in the secret war

The gadget makers

  • MI9, Britain’s escape service, helped prisoners of war escape and downed airmen get home. Its chief inventor was Christopher Clayton Hutton.
  • Escape maps were printed on silk: it doesn’t rustle, survives getting wet, and folds small enough to hide in a boot.
  • Tiny compasses were hidden inside buttons, pens and razors.
  • Maps, compasses and money were smuggled into prison camps hidden inside Monopoly boards, sent in parcels from fake charities.

Hiding a secret in plain sight: the same idea behind every cover story in the game.

Background: a WWII silk escape map. MI9 made maps like this; this one is American. Photo: CIA Museum, public domain.

MI9 was the British department that helped prisoners of war escape and helped airmen shot down over Europe get home. Its gadget makers, led by the inventive Christopher Clayton Hutton, came up with all sorts of tricks. Escape maps were printed on silk, like the one in the photo, which doesn't rustle when searched, survives water, and folds small enough to hide in a boot heel. This particular map was made by the American OSS, which copied the idea. Tiny compasses were hidden in buttons, pens and razors. Maps, compasses and real money were even smuggled into prison camps hidden inside Monopoly game boards, sent in parcels from made-up charities so the Germans wouldn't suspect them. Some prisoners used secret codes in their letters home to send information to Britain. It was all about hiding a secret in plain sight.

Navajo Marines on Saipan, June 1944. Photo: US National Archives, public domain.

More roles in the secret war

The Navajo Code Talkers

The US Marines needed a code the Japanese could never break, so they turned to the Navajo language.

  • 29 → about 400: twenty-nine Navajo Marines created the code in 1942. About 400 served as code talkers.
  • Never broken: at Iwo Jima they sent more than 800 messages in two days without an error.
  • Kept secret until 1968. In 2001 the original 29 received the Congressional Gold Medal.
This story isn't in the game, but it is one of the great codebreaking stories of the war, and in this one the code was never broken. This photo shows Navajo Marines on Saipan in June 1944. In 1942, twenty-nine Navajo recruits in the US Marines created a code based on their language, with code words for military terms, like "iron fish" for submarine. About 400 Navajo eventually served as code talkers in the Pacific. At Iwo Jima, six code talkers sent and received more than 800 messages in the first two days of the battle without a mistake. The program stayed classified until 1968, and in 2001 the original 29 were awarded the Congressional Gold Medal. Code talkers from other nations, including the Comanche and Choctaw, served too.

 · An unsolved mystery

The message nobody can read

2012

A man cleaning a chimney in Bletchingley, England, found the skeleton of a pigeon. Tied to its leg was a small red canister with a coded message from World War II.

Still unsolved

The message is 27 groups of five letters. Britain’s codebreakers at GCHQ said they could not decode it without the original codebook.

Pigeons at war

Thousands of pigeons carried messages in World War II, and 32 received the Dickin Medal for animal bravery.

Discuss: why might a code that was used only once be impossible to break?

Here is a real codebreaking mystery that is still unsolved. In 2012, a man cleaning a chimney in a house in Bletchingley, England, found the skeleton of a pigeon with a small red canister on its leg. Inside was a coded message from World War II: 27 groups of five letters. Britain's codebreakers at GCHQ, the modern descendant of Bletchley Park, tried and said they could not read it without the original codebook. Pigeons carried many messages in the war, and 32 were awarded the Dickin Medal, a medal for animal bravery. Discussion question: why might a code that was only used once be almost impossible to break? It connects to the game: a cipher is only as safe as its key.

YOUR TURN

Every one of these people faced the same question.

How do you use a secret without losing it?

Which story surprised you most? Hold on to it, then play Codebreakers: The Hidden War.

Remember the facts, too. In the game, some classmates will be double agents, and real history is how you catch them.

Every person in this lesson faced the same problem: a secret is only useful if you use it, but using it can give it away. Ask students which story surprised them most, and have a couple share. Then move on to the game, where they will face that question themselves: how do you use a secret without losing it? One more thing to tell them: in the game's Trust or Traitor part, some classmates will secretly be double agents who plant one false fact in their intel reports. Facts from this lesson, like Garbo's 27 imaginary agents or where Operation Mincemeat pointed the Germans, can help them catch a lie, just as real intelligence officers checked reports against what they knew.
